title: Meet the Pins
summary: Look along the top and bottom edges of your Arduino Uno.

steps.title: Meet the Pins
steps.markdownContent: The Uno has digital pins for HIGH/LOW signals, analog pins for measurements, and power pins. Some digital pins have a ~ mark for PWM. Pins 0 and 1 are also used for serial communication.

quickCheck.question: Why does an Arduino have little pin holes along its edges?
options: To plug in jumper wires to connect circuits
To let cool air blow through
quickCheck.explanation: Pin headers let you plug jumper wires in so the Arduino can communicate with your circuits!
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Pins are tiny sockets where wires plug in, connecting the Arduino brain to lights and sensors.

quickCheck.question: What does the letter 'A' stand for on pins labeled A0 through A5?
quickCheck.explanation: The 'A' stands for Analog! Pins A0 to A5 read smooth, continuous signals from sensors.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Labels give us helpful clues. 'A' stands for Analog, designed for reading smooth ranges.

steps.title: Pin Headers & Specialized Channels
steps.markdownContent: Use the board labels as your map: digital for switches and outputs, analog for changing sensor measurements, power and GND for the circuit.

steps.title: Pin Inspection & Matching Challenge
steps.markdownContent: Find digital pin 13, analog pin A0, 5V, and GND. Match each label to the right part of the board.

steps.title: Pin Mastery Checkpoint
steps.markdownContent: Check how well you know the pin headers on the Arduino Uno!

interactiveConfig.question: What do the wavy tildes (~) next to digital pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11 mean?
options: They support PWM for simulating analog fading and speed control
They are broken and cannot be used
They are only for playing underwater
interactiveConfig.explanation: The tilde (~) indicates Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) capable pins that can simulate variable analog outputs.
